clue.text: They're most absorbing

parts.note: reads like praise for gripping books or films, but means the things that soak up the most liquid

explanation.surface: A recommendation of the most gripping entertainments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Absorbing' suggests fascinating; take it literally, as soaking up water, and the bath-time item appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Porous bath items are prized for how much water they can soak up.

clue.text: Such upsets may, have light consequences

definitions.text: Such upsets may, have light consequences

parts.words: Such upsets may, have light consequences
parts.note: an upset is a knocked-over drink, and the same word names thin tapers used to light fires or pipes

explanation.surface: Minor accidents can have trivial results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' looks like 'slight'; but the word for upsets (knocked-over liquids) also means paper or wood tapers used to light a fire.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both accidental upsets of liquid and slips of wood used for lighting.

clue.text: Cleopatra was interested in the colour of her hair

definitions.text: Cleopatra was interested in the colour of her hair

parts.words: Cleopatra was interested in the colour of her hair
parts.note: in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra the queen quizzes a messenger about Antony's new Roman wife, including her hair

explanation.surface: The Egyptian queen's curiosity about another woman's looks.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare, Cleopatra asks the messenger about the looks of Octavius Caesar's sister, whom Antony has married, ending with 'the colour of her hair'.
explanation.definitionFit: Antony's Roman wife, sister of Octavius, is Cleopatra's rival in Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: But not where tailors buy their irons at Michaelmas

definitions.text: But not where tailors buy their irons at Michaelmas

parts.words: But not where tailors buy their irons at Michaelmas
parts.note: a tailor's pressing iron is called a goose, so a market for geese sounds like where tailors would shop, though it is really an autumn festival

explanation.surface: A denial that tailors shop for pressing irons in late September.
explanation.walkthrough: A tailor's heavy smoothing iron is a 'goose'. Nottingham's Goose Fair, a famous English autumn funfair, began as a market for geese near Michaelmas (29 September), not for irons.
explanation.definitionFit: Nottingham's historic October funfair grew from a market where geese were sold.

clue.text: Folders for rising paper-hangers ?

parts.note: folders suggests stationery for papers, but here means fold-up frames that decorators climb when hanging wallpaper

explanation.surface: Files for wallpaper fitters on the way up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Folders' and 'paper' suggest office stationery; these folders are folding frames that decorators climb to hang wallpaper high on walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorators climb these folding, freestanding frames to reach high wall areas.

clue.text: A girl can make one by joining the force

definitions.text: A girl can make one by joining the force

parts.words: A girl can make one by joining the force
parts.note: a pretty woman (a fair one, in old usage) who joins the police becomes a good-looking officer, read as a phrase

explanation.surface: A young woman's career choice: becoming a police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair cop' is the British catchphrase of a caught criminal admitting arrest is justified; read literally, it is a fair (pretty) cop, which a girl becomes by joining the force (the police).
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a criminal's admission that an arrest is deserved, but literally names an attractive police officer.

clue.text: Well, it's a bit of an old poem

definitions.text: a bit of an old poem

explanation.surface: A remark that something is a fragment of an ancient verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Well means healthy, in good shape; the word also names a canto or section of an old ballad.

clue.text: Try following this river-it's hard work

definitions.text: Try following this river-it's hard work

parts.words: Try following this river-it's hard work
parts.note: the river's name with the word try after it spells a word for diligent toil

explanation.surface: A warning that tracing a river's course is tiring.
explanation.walkthrough: Put TRY after the name of this Asian river and you get INDUSTRY, which means hard work; 'following' places TRY after it.
explanation.definitionFit: This great river of Pakistan, followed by try, makes a word for diligence.

clue.text: A capital framework

parts.note: capital sounds like a city or excellent, but here is read as of the head, so the bony frame is the skull

explanation.surface: An excellent structure, or the layout of a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' comes from Latin caput, head; the head's framework is the skull.
explanation.definitionFit: The skull is the bony case of the head, the body's 'capital'.

clue.text: Inclination to be a songwriter ?

explanation.surface: A wish to compose music.
explanation.definitionFit: A liking or bent is one sense; split as pen chant it means writing a song.

clue.text: Does he attend think-ins?

parts.note: a think-in sounds like a conference, but here it means thinking inward, the habit of an inward-looking person

explanation.surface: A question about who goes to brainstorming sessions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Think-ins' looks like a sit-in or teach-in gathering; read as thinking inwards, it describes a person absorbed in their own thoughts.
explanation.definitionFit: A shy, self-absorbed person turns thoughts inward rather than outward toward others.

clue.text: The way of a runaway

parts.note: a runaway sounds like an escaped person, but here it is water running away down a pipe or channel

explanation.surface: How a fugitive makes their escape.
explanation.walkthrough: The runaway is not a fugitive but waste water, whose route out is a pipe or gutter.
explanation.definitionFit: Waste water flows away through a pipe or channel in a sink or street.

clue.text: Reception on the waterfront?

explanation.surface: A party held by the harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: A royal morning reception is one sense; the other is an embankment beside a river, a riverside quay.

clue.text: Object of amorous laughter

parts.note: alludes to the proverb that love laughs at the craftsman who makes and opens locks, since lovers get through any barrier

explanation.surface: Someone that lovers giggle at.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'Love laughs at locksmiths' says no lock can keep lovers apart; so this craftsman is what love laughs at.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb names this tradesman, who fits and opens locks, as the target of love's laughter.

clue.text: Local governors

parts.note: plainly describes elected members of a town or county authority

explanation.surface: People who run a district.
explanation.definitionFit: Elected members of a town or county authority govern their locality.

clue.text: Adam meets more than his match on stage

definitions.text: Adam meets more than his match on stage

parts.words: Adam meets more than his match on stage
parts.note: Adam is the first human male, and someone more than his match is a being above humanity; 'on stage' points to a play title

explanation.surface: The first man is outclassed in a theatre performance.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the title of a George Bernard Shaw play: Adam stands for an ordinary human male, and 'more than his match' for a being beyond human.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's comedy title pairs an ordinary male with Nietzsche's idea of a higher being.

clue.text: Furious ladies, but so gracious !

explanation.surface: Angry women who are nonetheless very kind.
explanation.walkthrough: The Furies of Greek myth were addressed as the Eumenides, 'the kindly ones', to avoid angering them.
explanation.definitionFit: The avenging Furies were named by the Greeks with a Greek word meaning kindly or gracious ones.

clue.text: It ruins neatness

parts.note: neatness looks like tidiness, but here a neat drink is undiluted spirit, spoiled by adding water

explanation.surface: Something that spoils tidiness.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'neat' drink is spirit with nothing added; watering it down ends that neatness.
explanation.definitionFit: Watering down a spirit makes it no longer neat, that is, undiluted.

clue.text: Sammoc

parts.note: the nonsense word is a familiar punctuation word written back to front

explanation.surface: A single nonsense word.
explanation.walkthrough: SAMMOC is COMMAS written backwards, i.e. turned upside down or inverted, which is also the British name for quotation marks.
explanation.definitionFit: Quotation marks are called this in Britain because they look like upside-down commas.

clue.text: Material assistance to those with something to hide

definitions.text: Material assistance to those with something to hide

parts.words: Material assistance to those with something to hide
parts.note: material assistance sounds like money or aid, but here is cloth that conceals, as gauze over a face

explanation.surface: Practical help given to people with secrets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Material assistance' suggests financial help; here it is fine fabric that covers or conceals a face.
explanation.definitionFit: Light fabric used for face coverings helps conceal whoever wears it.

clue.text: What's done to an ice to make it poisonous ?

definitions.text: What's done to an ice to make it poisonous ?

indicators.note: something is done to the words, so their letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A question of how to turn a frozen treat toxic.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearranging AN ICE TO (the 'What's done to') makes the poisonous plant monkshood, so the whole clue is both recipe and description.
explanation.definitionFit: Monkshood or wolfsbane is a highly toxic plant, so it makes things deadly.

clue.text: Claiming them need not evoke a one-sided argument

definitions.text: Claiming them need not evoke a one-sided argument

parts.words: Claiming them need not evoke a one-sided argument
parts.note: plays on the word for entitlements also being the plural of a side opposite left, so claiming them is not one-sided

explanation.surface: Asserting entitlements needn't start a lopsided debate.
explanation.walkthrough: Claiming one's entitlements might sound like taking only one side (the right side); the plural suggests both are fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Entitlements a person may claim are their just dues under law.

clue.text: French article, a silver variety, from this provider?

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; with this noun it forms the old name for a shop selling every kind of goods

parts.note: un is the French indefinite article, meaning a

indicators.note: a variety of a silver means the letters arranged in another form

explanation.surface: A French item, a type of silver, sold by some supplier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety' scrambles A SILVER to give IVERSAL after UN. A 'universal provider' was the old name for a department store stocking everything, so the answer completes 'provider'.
explanation.definitionFit: An old general store selling everything was called a universal provider, the adjective meaning all-embracing.

clue.text: Hardly an appropriate alias for Irene

definitions.text: Hardly an appropriate alias for Irene

indicators.note: an alias is another name, so the letters of the name are reworked into a different one

explanation.surface: A nickname that doesn't suit a woman called Irene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alias for' reshuffles IRENE into a man's name, which hardly suits a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a male given name, so it would be an unsuitable false name for a woman.

clue.text: She has no aim to confuse

indicators.note: these words are to be confused, so their letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman without any ambition muddles things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to confuse' scrambles NO AIM into a woman's name from the Bible's Book of Ruth.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical mother-in-law of Ruth bears this female name, so 'she' covers it.

clue.text: It's 9-1 on, he did not bless the inventor of the wheel

definitions.text: he did not bless the inventor of the wheel

parts.note: IX is nine in Roman numerals
I is one in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Odds of nine to one on, and a man who cursed whoever invented the wheel.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Ixion was punished by Zeus by being bound to a fiery wheel for eternity, so he had no reason to bless its inventor.
explanation.definitionFit: A mythical Greek king tied for ever to a burning wheel would curse that device's inventor.

clue.text: One to take part in a sea-fight ?

definitions.text: One to take part in a sea-fight ?

parts.words: One to take part in a sea-fight ?
parts.note: a sea-fight suggests a naval battle, but read as a fight with blades under the sea it points to a fish with a long sharp bill

explanation.surface: A sailor joining a naval battle.
explanation.walkthrough: A naval battle is the obvious picture; the creature that could fence underwater is the fish with a blade-like snout.
explanation.definitionFit: This large ocean fish has an upper jaw extended into a long flat blade.

clue.text: What MPs do in Opposition !

parts.note: doing in opposition suggests attacking the government, but MPs literally take their seats on the opposition benches

explanation.surface: A gibe at what opposition politicians actually achieve.
explanation.walkthrough: MPs are British Members of Parliament; the gibe is that in opposition they merely occupy seats on the benches.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Parliament take their seats in the House during a session.

clue.text: For this, one couldn't care less

definitions.text: For this, one couldn't care less

parts.words: For this, one couldn't care less
parts.note: 'couldn't care less' usually means indifference, but here it literally means giving the least possible care

explanation.surface: An expression of total indifference.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'couldn't care less' literally: giving no care at all to something is a failure of attention.
explanation.definitionFit: Failing to look after something means giving it no care or attention.

clue.text: Chekhov's trio

parts.note: points to the Russian playwright's drama about three siblings, Olga, Masha and Irina

explanation.surface: A threesome from the Russian dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: Chekhov's play 'Three Sisters' follows three women longing to return to Moscow.
explanation.definitionFit: The trio in Chekhov's play are female siblings, as its title says.
